summary: Defines extensions to the Internet SNMP MIB for managing DECnet Phase IV, the networking protocol suite from Digital Equipment Corporation. It lets SNMP management software inspect DECnet nodes. It was replaced by RFC 1559.

eli5.summary: A dictionary that lets a general network tool ask questions of old Digital company computers. It lists the facts those computers can report so any monitoring program can read them.

questions: how do i monitor decnet networks
subtitle: SNMP management objects for DECnet Phase IV networks

tldr.problem: Network managers needed to monitor and manage DECnet Phase IV networks (Digital Equipment Corporation's network protocol suite) using SNMP, which was becoming the standard for TCP/IP network management.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1289 defines SNMP managed objects for DECnet Phase IV, organized into groups for system state, sessions, end-to-end communication, routing, circuits, and other components. This allows IP-based management stations to monitor DECnet nodes integrated into TCP/IP networks.
tldr.outcome: The DECnet Phase IV MIB enabled integrated management of mixed TCP/IP and DECnet networks. It was replaced by RFC 1559 as DECnet and the protocol landscape evolved.

facts.label: Major groups
facts.value: System, Session, End, Routing, Circuit, Counters, Adjacency, Area

today: RFC 1289 has been obsoleted by RFC 1559. DECnet Phase IV networks are historically significant but no longer widely deployed; they have been superseded by TCP/IP networking. This MIB is retained for reference only.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1289 defines extensions to the SNMP MIB for managing DECnet Phase IV, the networking protocol suite developed by Digital Equipment Corporation. DECnet Phase IV was widely deployed alongside TCP/IP in enterprise networks during the 1980s and 1990s. This RFC makes it possible for IP-based network management stations to monitor and manage DECnet nodes as part of an integrated network management strategy.

The document defines managed objects derived from the Digital Network Architecture (DNA) Network Management Functional Specification Version 4.0.0. These objects are organized into groups corresponding to the major functional areas of DECnet Phase IV: system control, session management, end-to-end communication, routing, circuits, data-link control, and adjacency tracking.
sections.eli5: This is about managing old Digital computers on a network. Instead of using Digital's own management tools, you can use the same SNMP tools you use for regular networks.

sections.title: System and Management Groups
sections.content:
The System Group defines the overall state of a DECnet executor (the DECnet software running on a particular node). The phivSystemState object tracks whether the executor is ON (allowing new logical links), OFF (terminating existing links and blocking routing), SHUT (blocking new links but maintaining existing ones until they close naturally), or RESTRICTED (blocking new incoming links). These states allow administrators to gracefully shut down DECnet services.

The Network Management Group provides version information about the node's DECnet management software, including version number, Engineering Change Order (ECO) number, and user ECO number. This helps managers understand what management capabilities are available on a given node.

The Session Layer Group defines timers for session establishment: phivSessionInTimer (the wait for a process to accept an incoming connection) and phivSessionOutTimer (the wait for an outgoing connection to be acknowledged).
sections.eli5: The system group is like the main power switch and status lights. It says whether the DECnet service is running, shutting down, or blocking new connections.

sections.title: End-to-End Communication and Session Tracking
sections.content:
The End Communication Layer Group tracks logical links and sessions between the local node and remote DECnet nodes. The End Remote Table contains one entry per known remote node, recording the node's DECnet address, operational state, the circuit used to reach it, the number of active logical links, and the average round-trip delay.

The End Count Table provides detailed counters for each remote node: user data bytes and messages sent and received, total bytes and messages (including protocol overhead), the number of connection attempts, response timeouts, and connection resource errors. The phivEndCountSecsLastZeroed counter indicates when these counters were last reset.

Additional end-layer objects control maximum active links, retransmission behavior (timeout factor, delay factor, delay weighting), and an inactivity timer that triggers heartbeat messages to test idle links. A counter tracks the high-water mark of concurrent links.
sections.eli5: The end layer watches each connection to a remote DECnet computer: how many messages were sent and received, how fast it responds, and whether it is still alive.

sections.title: Routing Layer Parameters
sections.content:
The Routing Layer Group defines parameters that control how DECnet packets are routed through the network. These include maximum path cost and hop count limits, which define when a node is considered unreachable; buffer sizes for routing buffers and segment buffers (for the end-to-end layer); the maximum number of nodes the executor can be aware of in its area; and limits on the number of routers and nonrouters that can be known on Ethernet circuits.

Additional objects track broadcast route update timers (controlling how often routing information is refreshed), maximum number of circuits, and maximum visits (the maximum number of hops a message can traverse before being discarded). The Routing Version object reports the version of the DECnet routing software.

These parameters allow administrators to tune routing behavior for different network topologies and sizes, balancing between keeping routes fresh and minimizing routing overhead.
sections.eli5: Routing parameters are like speed limits and distance markers on a highway. They say how many hops is too many, what is the farthest cost to allow, and how often to update the route maps.

sections.title: Circuit and Data Link Groups
sections.content:
The RFC defines groups for managing lower-layer protocol details: the Circuit Group (defining circuits and their properties), the DDCMP Group (for DECnet Data Communications Message Protocol, a data-link protocol), the Ethernet Group (for Ethernet circuits), the Line Group (for line-specific parameters), and the Non-Broadcast Line Group (for point-to-point circuits).

The Counters Group provides comprehensive statistics at various protocol levels. The Adjacency Group tracks neighboring DECnet nodes and maintains adjacency tables. The Area Group manages DECnet area-level information, allowing administrators to organize networks into areas for scalability.

These groups allow detailed monitoring of network topology, circuit status, error counts, and data-link performance across various media and protocols.
sections.eli5: These groups track the wires (circuits), the protocols running on them (like Ethernet or dial-up lines), and the neighbors you are directly connected to.

sections.title: Status and Compatibility
sections.content:
RFC 1289 was published in December 1991 as a Proposed Standard. It was produced by the DECnet Phase IV MIB working group of the Internet Engineering Task Force.

RFC 1289 has been obsoleted by RFC 1559, which provides updated DECnet MIB definitions. DECnet Phase IV networks are largely historical; they have been superseded by IP networks and more modern protocols. This MIB should not be used for new implementations; it is retained for reference and legacy systems.
sections.eli5: This RFC is from 1991 and is no longer used. RFC 1559 took its place. DECnet is history; everything uses IP now.
